{{distinguish|text = [[Wigner%27s_theorem#Modifications_and_generalizations|Kadison's theorem generalizing]] Wigner's theorem}}

In [[mathematics]], '''Kadison transitivity theorem''' is a result in the theory of [[C*-algebras]] that, in effect, asserts the equivalence of the notions of topological irreducibility and [[Irreducible representation|algebraic irreducibility]] of representations of C*-algebras. It implies that, for irreducible representations of C*-algebras, the only non-zero linear invariant subspace is the whole space.

The theorem, proved by [[Richard Kadison]], was surprising as ''a priori'' there is no reason to believe that all topologically irreducible representations are also algebraically irreducible.

==Statement==
A family <math>\mathcal{F}</math> of [[bounded operator]]s on a [[Hilbert space]] <math>\mathcal{H}</math> is said to act ''topologically irreducibly'' when <math>\{0\}</math> and <math>\mathcal{H}</math> are the only closed stable subspaces under <math>\mathcal{F}</math>. The family <math>\mathcal{F}</math> is said to act ''algebraically irreducibly'' if <math>\{0\}</math> and <math>\mathcal{H}</math> are the only linear manifolds in <math>\mathcal{H}</math> stable under <math>\mathcal{F}</math>.

'''Theorem'''. <ref>Theorem 5.4.3; [[Kadison, R. V.]]; [[Ringrose, J. R.]], ''Fundamentals of the Theory of Operator Algebras'', Vol. I : Elementary Theory, {{ISBN|978-0821808191}}</ref> If the C*-algebra <math>\mathfrak{A}</math> acts topologically irreducibly on the Hilbert space <math>\mathcal{H}, \{ y_1, \cdots, y_n \}</math> is a set of vectors and <math>\{x_1, \cdots, x_n \}</math> is a linearly independent set of vectors in <math>\mathcal{H}</math>, there is an <math>A</math> in <math>\mathfrak{A}</math> such that <math>Ax_j = y_j</math>. If <math>Bx_j = y_j</math> for some [[self-adjoint operator]] <math>B</math>, then <math>A</math> can be chosen to be self-adjoint.

'''Corollary'''. If the C*-algebra <math>\mathfrak{A}</math> acts topologically irreducibly on the Hilbert space <math>\mathcal{H}</math>, then it acts algebraically irreducibly.
